official_title: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring law enforcement to notify the department of homeland security when a person is charged with either a violent crime or any crime if the person has a prior felony conviction if law enforcement cannot determine that the person is lawfully present in the United States?
plain_summary: Requires police, jail staff, and prosecutors to tell the federal Department of Homeland Security within 72 hours when they charge someone with a violent crime, or with any crime if that person has a past felony conviction, and they can't confirm the person is legally in the U.S. It applies at the time of charging, before any trial.
yes_means: Law enforcement must notify federal immigration authorities after filing certain criminal charges against people not confirmed to be lawfully present.
no_means: Current law stays: Colorado allows cooperation with federal immigration authorities in some criminal matters but limits state and local involvement in civil immigration enforcement.
current_law: Colorado law lets state and local law enforcement help enforce federal criminal law but limits their role in civil immigration enforcement. Agencies and employees generally may not share certain nonpublic personal information with federal immigration authorities unless required by federal law, a court order, or a judicial warrant; violations can bring fines up to $50,000. No federal or state law currently requires notifying immigration authorities when someone is charged. Local rules vary: Denver bars federal immigration agents from city property like courthouses; El Paso County requires officers to notify federal authorities about people in custody they suspect lack legal status.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: state spending rises in 2026-27 for system updates ($50,000 at the Department of Revenue to access federal databases, $10,000 at Natural Resources), assumed paid from the General Fund. Workload also rises for several state departments. Most of the added work falls on local district attorney offices, which must determine a charged person's immigration status and communicate with the federal government; amounts vary by county.
confusing_wording_note: The title packs three 'if' conditions into one sentence. Read it as: notify DHS when (a) a person is charged, AND (b) the charge is violent OR the person has any prior felony, AND (c) police can't confirm the person is here legally. It triggers at charging, not conviction. 'Cannot determine' means people whose status is simply unknown after a 'reasonable effort' are included, not only people confirmed to be undocumented.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say violent individuals and repeat offenders who are here unlawfully should be reported to federal authorities, that the measure targets public-safety threats rather than law-abiding immigrants, and that it replaces a patchwork of local policies with one statewide standard.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it undermines due process by reporting people to ICE before any court finds them guilty, that legally present people could be swept up if they can't prove status within 72 hours, and that undefined terms like 'reasonable effort' invite profiling and erode trust so that immigrants stop reporting crimes.

official_title: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating new law granting the right for consumers to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses and for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas to consumers?
plain_summary: Puts a right to buy natural gas for cooking and heating, and a right for utilities to sell it, into the state constitution. The Blue Book says this may limit the ability of state and local governments to enforce current or future rules that restrict natural gas, such as building codes that require all-electric new homes.
yes_means: Creates a state constitutional right to buy and sell natural gas for use in homes and businesses.
no_means: Keeps current law and regulations on the purchase and sale of natural gas.
current_law: The state Public Utilities Commission regulates investor-owned gas utilities, including rates, safety, and 'clean heat plans'; in December 2025 it required those utilities to plan for a 41% cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035 vs. 2015. The state health department sets emissions standards for gas appliances. Local governments can regulate gas installation and several towns (for example Crested Butte) now require electric heating and appliances in new residential buildings.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: may minimally increase state spending, mainly at the Department of Local Affairs to revise technical assistance on building codes, and more workload and legal costs for the PUC, Natural Resources, Public Health and Environment, and the Energy Office. Local governments with or considering gas-restricting building codes may face legal costs to conform their codes and change permitting and inspection.
confusing_wording_note: The title says 'creating new law granting the right,' which is accurate but doesn't tell you the practical effect: the Blue Book says the constitutional right 'may limit' state and local rules restricting gas, including existing emissions targets and local electrification codes. A yes vote is as much about limiting future regulation as about any right you lack today (nobody is currently barred from buying gas).

supporters_case.text: Supporters say natural gas is affordable, reliable, and the primary heating source for most Colorado households, especially in extreme cold, and that the measure guarantees continued access without state or local interference.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say burning gas adds to climate change and air pollution and shouldn't be protected in the constitution, that it would limit efforts to cut emissions and adopt wind, solar, and geothermal, and that local communities should keep the power to set their own energy and health priorities.

official_title: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating a constitutional right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods, including all species of fish and wildlife managed by the state except non-game species, endangered species, or any species that is illegal to hunt under federal law, and, in connection therewith, establishing hunting and fishing as the preferred means of managing fish and wildlife populations; and preserving the right of the state to regulate hunting, fishing, and wildlife management if necessary for sound scientific wildlife conservation and management, public safety, or to preserve the future of hunting and fishing opportunities for all species?
plain_summary: Adds a right to hunt and fish 'by traditional methods' to the state constitution and declares hunting and fishing the 'preferred' way to manage wildlife populations. It makes no immediate change to any hunting or fishing rule; the state can still regulate for science, safety, or to preserve future hunting. The Blue Book says its effect depends on how courts read it when future rules are challenged.
yes_means: Creates a state constitutional right to hunt and fish.
no_means: Hunting and fishing continue as allowed under existing state and federal law, with no new constitutional right.
current_law: Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) manages fish and wildlife and its citizen Commission, appointed by the Governor, sets hunting and fishing rules: where and when, licenses, methods, and bag limits. State law already requires wildlife to be protected and managed for the use and enjoyment of residents and visitors. There is no constitutional right to hunt or fish today; 24 other states have one.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: no significant change to state spending in the near term, but CPW could see higher legal costs when writing rules to comply with the new right and higher litigation costs if existing or future regulations are challenged. The amount can't be estimated because it depends on lawsuits and court decisions.
confusing_wording_note: The long title lists exceptions (non-game, endangered, federally protected species) and a state power to regulate, which makes it sound like nothing changes. The operative words are 'preferred means of managing' wildlife. That phrase could matter later if voters or CPW try to restrict a practice like trapping or a particular hunt; the Blue Book notes 'traditional methods' and 'preferred' are not defined.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say the amendment is lasting protection against future efforts to restrict or ban hunting and fishing, that 24 states already have such a right, that hunting and fishing are part of Colorado's heritage and economy, and that license sales fund about a third of CPW's budget (about $115 million a year).

opponents_case.text: Opponents say the constitution should protect fundamental rights, not recreation; that Colorado already leads on wildlife management; that elevating one method above others could block reasonable guardrails on hunting, fishing, and trapping; and that vague language invites costly lawsuits against rules voters and CPW already put in place.

official_title: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring a voter to sign and include the last four digits of their social security number or their Colorado driver's license or identification card number on the outside of their mail ballot for any federal or state election, and, in connection therewith, allowing the voter to correct missing or incorrect information, including with alternative forms of identification; and prohibiting a county clerk and recorder from counting the mail ballot unless the problem is fixed?
plain_summary: Adds an ID step to mail voting. On top of signing the envelope, you would write the last four digits of your Social Security number, Colorado driver's license, or Colorado ID number on the outside of the envelope for state and federal elections. If it's missing or doesn't match, the county must contact you and you'd have 8 days after Election Day to fix it, including with a passport, military ID, or tribal ID. In-person ID rules don't change.
yes_means: Voters must provide identification information with their mail ballot, in addition to their signature.
no_means: Mail ballots keep the current signature-only verification system.
current_law: Every Colorado voter is mailed a ballot and must sign the return envelope. Judges compare that signature to the one on file from registration and DMV records. If it looks wrong, two judges from different parties must agree, then the county contacts the voter, who has 8 days after Election Day to confirm identity or the ballot isn't counted. In 2024, 92% of Colorado ballots were mail ballots, mostly returned by drop box.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: up to $2.7 million in added state and local spending in 2026-27 and $1.2 million a year after that, for voter outreach, printing, and staff time verifying numbers. Counties bear up to $2.5 million the first year (about 45% reimbursed by the state). The Secretary of State's share may be covered by raising business filing fees.
confusing_wording_note: This is a measure about how you vote, voted on by mail. The title says 'on the outside of their mail ballot'; it means on the return envelope, where your signature already goes. It does not require a photo ID and does not change the ID list for in-person voting. Note that under the measure a Colorado DL or ID number only counts if the card is REAL ID compliant, a detail the title omits. Nothing changes for the November 2026 election itself.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say government ID numbers are more consistent and less subjective than signature matching, that most voters already have a qualifying ID or know their SSN, that anyone without one can still vote in person, and that the extra check builds public confidence.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it adds a burden without meaningfully improving security, that eligible voters could lose their vote over small mistakes, that people with privacy concerns or without the listed IDs would be pushed away from the state's most used voting method, and that signature verification already catches the rare ineligible ballot.

official_title: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning ballot question language, and, in connection therewith, requiring all state and local ballot questions to be written in plain language and at no more than an 8th grade reading level and prohibiting a state statute from requiring language that conflicts with these requirements in ballot questions for citizen-initiated measures?
plain_summary: Requires every state and local ballot title to be written in plain language at no higher than an 8th-grade reading level, and bars the legislature from passing laws that force extra language into citizen-initiative titles if that language conflicts with the plain-language rule. It doesn't define 'plain language' or say who decides whether a title meets the standard.
yes_means: Ballot titles must be written in plain language at an 8th-grade reading level, and no law may interfere with that requirement for citizen initiatives.
no_means: Current law stays: titles must be in plain language but no specific grade level is set, and the legislature can still require specific language in titles.
current_law: A three-member Title Board (Attorney General's office, Secretary of State's office, legislative legal staff) writes titles for citizen initiatives and must use plain language understandable to the widest audience, avoiding legal and technical terms where possible. The legislature writes titles for its own referred measures. Several current laws require extra title language, for example tax measures must state the dollar amount of the tax change and tax cuts must describe potential spending reductions.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: may minimally increase workload for the Title Board to update its plain-language standards and apply an 8th-grade reading-level test when setting titles.
confusing_wording_note: A measure about plain-language ballot titles whose own title is a 68-word sentence. The second half is the part with teeth: it would block statutes that require extra language in citizen-initiative titles, which today includes the all-caps 'SHALL STATE TAXES BE INCREASED $X' wording and tax-impact tables you see on Amendment 87. Supporters frame that as stopping legislative interference; opponents frame it as stripping voters of cost information. The 8th-grade rule applies to all ballot questions, but the anti-interference rule only protects citizen initiatives, not the legislature's own referred measures.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say a constitutional 8th-grade standard gives real guidance on what 'plain' means, helps voters understand complex measures, and stops future legislatures from writing laws that make initiative titles complicated or confusing.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say current law already requires plain titles, that an undefined constitutional standard will spawn more legal challenges to titles, and that it could prohibit laws adding information voters need, like the cost of a tax measure.

official_title: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning congressional redistricting, and, in connection therewith, reenacting the current process for congressional redistricting in the Colorado Constitution and prohibiting modifications to a final map unless at least three public meetings are held, the modifications do not have the effect of dividing communities of interest or purposefully favoring one political party, and are approved by the congressional redistricting commission and the Colorado Supreme Court?
plain_summary: Makes it harder to redraw Colorado's eight U.S. House districts between censuses. Any 'off-cycle' map change would need at least three public hearings, approval by the Independent Congressional Redistricting Commission, and adoption by the Colorado Supreme Court, and it couldn't intentionally favor a party or needlessly split communities. Regular once-a-decade redistricting is unchanged.
yes_means: The independent redistricting commission and the state Supreme Court must approve any new congressional districts proposed outside a scheduled redistricting year.
no_means: The current rules stay: the constitution sets a process for redistricting every ten years and is silent on mid-decade changes.
current_law: In 2018 voters created the Colorado Independent Congressional Redistricting Commission, which draws new districts after each census (last in 2021, next in 2031). The constitution does not set a process for changing maps between censuses. Since 2025 at least ten other states have redrawn congressional maps mid-decade.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: about $370,000 in Legislative Department costs in any year the commission has to convene off-cycle (staff, commissioner reimbursement, legal counsel), plus a small workload increase for the Judicial Department to review a map. No cost if no off-cycle redistricting is proposed.
confusing_wording_note: 'Reenacting the current process' sounds like a change but mostly restates what's already in the constitution; the new part is the set of hurdles for off-cycle changes. Note the sponsor: this was placed on the ballot by Advance Colorado, a conservative group, at a time when Democrats control the legislature, so the usual partisan cues may run the other way from what you'd expect. The Blue Book's 'against' argument is about preserving voters' flexibility, not about wanting gerrymandering.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say the measure protects public participation and transparency, keeps partisan politics out of mid-decade map changes, and affirms the voters' 2018 decision to use an independent commission at a time when politicians in other states are redrawing maps with little public input.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it creates an unnecessary constitutional barrier if Colorado voters ever want new districts mid-decade, whether in response to other states' partisan maps or changing priorities, and that the same commission that drew the maps shouldn't get a veto over changing them; voters should have the final word.

official_title: SHALL STATE TAXES BE INCREASED $2.7 BILLION ANNUALLY, IN ORDER TO INCREASE OR IMPROVE LEVELS OF PUBLIC SERVICES, INCLUDING K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL EDUCATION, HEALTH CARE, AND EARLY CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION SERVICES, BY AN AMENDMENT TO THE COLORADO CONSTITUTION AND A CHANGE TO THE COLORADO REVISED STATUTES REPEALING EXISTING LAW AND CREATING NEW LAW TO REPLACE THE UNIFORM STATE INCOME TAX RATE WITH A GRADUATED INCOME TAX STRUCTURE, AND, IN CONNECTION THEREWITH, AMENDING THE TAXPAYER'S BILL OF RIGHTS TO ELIMINATE THE CONSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENT FOR ALL TAXABLE NET INCOME TO BE TAXED AT ONE RATE WITH NO ADDED TAX ON INCOME; ESTABLISHING VARIOUS INCOME TAX RATES BASED ON THE AMOUNT OF TAXABLE INCOME EARNED BY INDIVIDUALS, ESTATES, TRUSTS, AND CORPORATIONS, WHILE MAINTAINING THE CURRENT 4.4% TAX ON INCOME FROM THE SALE OF A PRINCIPAL RESIDENCE, WHICH WILL RESULT IN THE ESTIMATED CHANGE IN INCOME TAXES OWED BY INDIVIDUALS AS IDENTIFIED IN THE FOLLOWING TABLE; AND AUTHORIZING THE STATE TO RETAIN AND SPEND ANY INCREASED REVENUE FROM THE NEW TAX STRUCTURE, AS A VOTER-APPROVED REVENUE CHANGE, TO SUPPLEMENT CURRENT LEVELS OF FUNDING FOR K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL EDUCATION, HEALTH CARE, AND EARLY CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION PROGRAMS?
plain_summary: Replaces Colorado's flat 4.4% income tax with six brackets starting in 2027: 3.7% on the first $25,000 of taxable income, 4.2% from $25,001 to $100,000, 4.4% from $100,001 to $500,000, then 7.4%, 7.9%, and 8.4% on income above $500,000, $750,000, and $1 million. Taxpayers with taxable income under about $510,000 pay less (up to $325 less); those above pay more. The extra money (about $2 billion a year) must go to K-12 schools, health care, and early childhood care and is exempt from the TABOR cap. Brackets are not adjusted for inflation.
yes_means: Creates a graduated state income tax that raises revenue, spends the extra on K-12 education, health care, and early childhood care and education, and exempts that money from the TABOR revenue limit.
no_means: Keeps the constitutional requirement for a single flat income tax rate (currently 4.4%).
current_law: Since 1987 Colorado has taxed all income at one flat rate; TABOR (Article X, Section 20 of the constitution) requires a single rate. The rate is 4.4%, approved by voters in 2022. Any tax rate increase already requires voter approval.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: raises state income tax revenue by an estimated $958.4 million in 2026-27 (half year) and $1.972 billion in 2027-28, growing with income and population. The $2.7 billion figure in the title is the legally required maximum estimate for the first full year. Average change by federal AGI: a cut of $1 to $325 for everyone under $1 million (for example, $194 less at $50,000 to $69,999; $325 less at $150,000 to $499,999); an average increase of $26,085 for the roughly 46,000 taxpayers with AGI of $1 million or more. No effect on current TABOR refunds or refund mechanisms. One-time $98,000 cost at the Department of Revenue. More state money flows to school districts, in amounts the legislature decides.
pass_threshold: Simple majority (constitutional amendment, but it only repeals existing constitutional language, so the 55% rule does not apply)
confusing_wording_note: Three traps. (1) The all-caps title and the words 'SHALL STATE TAXES BE INCREASED $2.7 BILLION' are required by law for any tax increase; the table underneath shows that the average taxpayer in every income band under $1 million would pay LESS. Read the table. (2) It conflicts with Proposition 136 (a 4.4% cap). If both pass, the one with more yes votes is generally expected to control, but the Blue Book says the result is legally unclear and the legislature or a court would have to sort it out. If you want a graduated tax, the consistent vote is Yes on 87 and No on 136; if you want to keep the flat tax, No on 87 and Yes on 136. (3) Unlike most amendments, this one needs only 50%+1, not 55%, because it repeals rather than adds constitutional text.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say the measure cuts taxes for 97% of taxpayers and raises them only on top earners who can afford it, that a graduated tax is fairer than a flat one because a dollar matters more at $30,000 than at $1 million, and that the money funds schools, health care, and child care at a time federal cuts threaten them. The federal government and 27 states already use graduated rates.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it is a multibillion-dollar tax increase that will make Colorado less competitive, push high earners and employers out, and over time pull more taxpayers into higher brackets because they aren't indexed to inflation; that the flat tax under TABOR is fair and predictable; and that the state should prioritize the money it already collects rather than permanently expand government.

official_title: Shall state investment in K-12 public education increase two percent each year for the next ten years, with investments used to increase teacher pay, improve teacher retention, lower class sizes, and increase access to career and technical courses, without raising taxes but instead funded by raising the annual limit on state fiscal year spending only by the amount spent on public K-12 education as a voter-approved revenue change, and requiring an annual publicly released, independent audit to show how the new investments are spent?
plain_summary: Lets the state keep money it would otherwise have to refund under TABOR, up to a new higher cap tied to what the state spends on K-12 schools. For the first ten years the kept money goes to K-12 (teacher pay and retention, smaller classes, career and technical courses, and more) and to programs for children such as preschool and child care; after ten years, a fixed amount goes to K-12 and the rest can be spent on anything the legislature chooses. It does not change tax rates. It is expected to eliminate TABOR refunds in 2027 and 2028.
yes_means: The state may keep some or all of the revenue that would otherwise be refunded under TABOR and must spend it on K-12 education, programs that support children, and (after ten years) any other purposes.
no_means: Current TABOR refunds and current funding levels for K-12 and children's programs stay as they are.
current_law: The Colorado Constitution (TABOR) caps how much revenue the state can keep each year, growing with inflation plus population. Money above the cap is refunded to taxpayers unless voters let the state keep it. The state may spend retained revenue only as voters approve.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: reduces TABOR refunds by $329.9 million in 2026-27 and $521.0 million in 2027-28, which eliminates refunds in both years. For example, a single filer with $75,000 AGI would get a $28 refund in 2027 under current law and $0 under NN; at $100,000, $68 in 2028 vs. $0. In some future years the measure could have no effect; in others it could reduce refunds by more than $1,000 per taxpayer. State spending rises by the same amounts: about $241.5 million to K-12 and $241.5 million to children's programs in year one. The first year's cap is $4.6 billion above the current TABOR limit, but only about $500 million is expected to actually be retained. Revenue is not expected to exceed the new NN cap for at least five to ten years.
confusing_wording_note: The title says 'without raising taxes' and 'increase two percent each year.' Both are true in a narrow sense and misleading in a broad one. No tax rate changes, but the Blue Book's own 'against' argument calls it 'essentially a tax increase' because you would stop getting TABOR refund checks (which show up as a credit on your state return). The '2% each year' is a spending floor for specific K-12 uses; the much bigger change is the new, permanently higher revenue cap. The title also doesn't mention that after ten years the money can go to 'any other purposes.' Finally, Proposition NN interacts with Proposition 137: if 137 also passes, there may be less (or no) money for NN to keep in some years.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say Colorado schools are underfunded by about $3.5 billion ($4,000 per pupil), that NN redirects money the state already collects to teacher pay, smaller classes, and career and technical education in every district with audits for accountability, and that the current cap doesn't keep up with the rising cost of educating and caring for children.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it is essentially a tax increase that permanently reduces or eliminates TABOR refunds, which are a taxpayer right; that it eventually hands the state over $5 billion a year; and that school funding is already up 25% in five years while enrollment falls, so the state should cut waste before taking more.

official_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes concerning criminal penalties for fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids, and, in connection therewith, increasing the felony classifications of drug-related crimes for distribution, manufacturing, dispensing, sale, or possession of fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids; creating mandated treatment for certain drug felony violations based on possession amount; and changing sentencing provisions to narrow or eliminate exemptions for crimes related to fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids and drug-related deaths?
plain_summary: Makes possession of any amount of fentanyl (or similar synthetic opioids) a felony, requires 8 to 32 years in prison for distributing any amount, and removes several ways judges can reduce penalties, including the 'didn't know it had fentanyl' defense and Good Samaritan protections in distribution cases. Possession under 1 gram can still be reduced to a misdemeanor if the person completes mandatory treatment.
yes_means: Possession of any amount of fentanyl becomes a felony, distribution of any amount carries a mandatory minimum 8-year prison sentence, and options to reduce penalties for certain possession and distribution offenses are eliminated.
no_means: Minor fentanyl possession stays a misdemeanor, felony distribution penalties stay tiered by quantity, and judges keep options to reduce penalties in certain cases.
current_law: Penalties depend on amount and intent. Distribution over 50 grams, to a minor, or of 4+ grams causing death: mandatory 8 to 32 years. Distribution of 4 to 50 grams: possible 4 to 8 years; under 4 grams: possible 2 to 4 years with reductions for Good Samaritan reporting. Possession of 1 to 4 grams: possible 6 months to 1 year with reductions. Possession under 1 gram: no prison (misdemeanor) unless multiple prior convictions. 'Amount' means the whole mixture, not pure fentanyl.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: state spending (courts, public defenders, prisons) rises by $0.9 million in year one, $8.9 million in year two, and an estimated $68.2 million by year five as more people serve longer sentences, with possible need for new prison space. Paid from the General Fund with no funding source specified. Small revenue increase from fines ($73,000 a year). County district attorney costs also rise.
confusing_wording_note: The title mentions 'creating mandated treatment,' which can read like a treatment-focused measure. The Blue Book table is clearer: every distribution tier becomes a mandatory 8 to 32 years, including under 4 grams, and the treatment provision is court-ordered treatment for sub-1-gram possession as a condition of reducing a felony to a misdemeanor. 'Narrow or eliminate exemptions' means removing the defenses that currently let someone who didn't know a pill contained fentanyl avoid the harshest charge.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say fentanyl is uniquely deadly and deserves tougher penalties, that mandatory prison for dealers disrupts distribution and keeps them off the street, gives victims' families a sense of justice, and that accountability for users may deter use and reduce overdose deaths.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say harsher penalties are unlikely to reduce use, crime, or overdoses; that fear of prison will keep people from seeking treatment or calling 911 during an overdose; that it treats people sharing trace amounts like major traffickers; and that long sentences are expensive and shift money from treatment and schools to an overcrowded prison system.

official_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law concerning human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude, and, in connection therewith, creating new law expanding human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude to include knowingly trading anything of monetary value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor and increasing the penalty to be life in prison without parole or release?
plain_summary: Raises the penalty for child sex trafficking from 8 to 48 years in prison (a class 2 felony) to mandatory life in prison without parole (a class 1 felony), with no judicial discretion. It also expands the crime to include buying sexual activity with a minor, so buyers as well as sellers would get a life sentence.
yes_means: Child sex trafficking carries life in prison without parole, and the crime is expanded to include buying sexual activity with a minor.
no_means: Child sex trafficking stays a class 2 felony with 8 to 48 years in prison plus 5 years of mandatory parole.
current_law: Human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude is a class 2 felony: 8 to 48 years in prison and 5 years mandatory parole. A minor legally cannot consent to commercial sex. Current law provides defenses and protections for people charged with this crime who are themselves trafficking victims. Buyers can be charged under other sex crimes.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: added prison costs begin in about 14 years, when offenders would otherwise have been paroled: about $180,000 in 2041-42, rising by roughly that amount each year for several years, before leveling off. Not adjusted for inflation; medical costs for aging inmates grow separately. Minimal added court and DA workload because cases with harsher penalties take longer. Paid from the General Fund with no funding source specified.
confusing_wording_note: 'Modifying existing law' and 'expanding' understate the scale: this moves one crime from the second-highest felony class to the highest, with a single mandatory sentence (life without parole) and no range. The expansion to 'knowingly trading anything of monetary value to buy' sexual activity with a minor means a first-time buyer would face the same mandatory life sentence as a trafficker. The Blue Book's 'against' argument raises the risk that trafficking victims who are coerced into recruiting others could face the life sentence too.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say child sex trafficking causes lifelong harm and deserves a life sentence rather than a shorter term or probation, that a clear, definite punishment ensures offenders cannot hurt more children, deters the crime, and gives victims certainty that justice is served.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say harsher sentences are unlikely to deter trafficking, that victims who are forced to help traffickers could face life in prison and become less willing to report or cooperate, that judges lose the ability to weigh the facts, and that the measure prioritizes punishment over prevention.

official_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law restricting participation in all K-12 and collegiate school sports based on the participant's sex as determined by certain aspects of their biological reproductive system, and, in connection therewith, requiring a school, institution of higher education, or athletic association to designate each school or intramural athletic team or sport as male, female, or coeducational; only allowing participants to compete on the team or sport of their designated sex or to compete on a coeducational team; creating an exception to allow a female to participate on a male-designated team or sport if there is no female team available; prohibiting a government entity, licensing or accrediting organization, or athletic association from entertaining a complaint, opening an investigation, or taking other adverse action against a school for maintaining separate teams or sports for females; and providing the commissioner of education with the authority to enforce the proposed initiative for K-12 school districts?
plain_summary: Requires every school sports team, from elementary school through college and including intramurals and school-sponsored after-school programs at public, private, charter, and religious schools, to be designated male, female, or coed, with 'male' and 'female' defined by reproductive biology (sperm vs. egg production). Students may play only on the team matching their biological sex or on a coed team; girls may join a boys' team if there is no girls' team. Schools set their own verification methods. No agency or athletic association may investigate or punish a school for keeping a female-only team. The state education commissioner enforces it for public K-12 districts; there is no enforcement mechanism for private schools or colleges.
yes_means: All school-based teams must be designated for biological males, biological females, or mixed, and schools and districts must adopt sex-eligibility policies for sports.
no_means: Schools, districts, and athletic associations keep setting their own eligibility policies within current state and federal law.
current_law: The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act bars discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression, and public schools and colleges may not exclude students from extracurriculars that match their gender identity. CHSAA (high school sports) recognizes transgender athletes' right to participate and in December 2025 settled a lawsuit by agreeing not to penalize schools that keep sex-separated teams. NCAA rules limit women's competition to athletes assigned female at birth. Federal Executive Order 14201 (Feb. 2025) directs agencies to read Title IX as barring biological males from female teams; in June 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Title IX permits states to separate sports by biological sex. The Blue Book says it is unclear how the measure would interact with CADA.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: indeterminate increase in Department of Education workload and legal costs if a district refuses to comply and the commissioner must act; state colleges have costs to update policies (paid from tuition, fees, or athletics revenue); minimal costs for schools and districts to update and implement policies, potentially more if the state takes remedial action.
confusing_wording_note: The 163-word title never uses the word 'transgender,' but that is the policy question: whether transgender students can play on teams matching their gender identity. The scope is wider than varsity: it covers intramurals, after-school programs, elementary school, and private and religious schools. 'Certain aspects of their biological reproductive system' means the measure's sperm/egg definition, and the measure does not say how schools should verify sex, which both sides flag (supporters as flexibility, opponents as 'body inspection' risk). It is a statute, so the legislature could amend it later without another vote.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say females should compete against females, that biological males on female teams create unfair advantages that cost girls wins, records, and scholarships, that physical differences raise safety and locker-room privacy concerns, and that a single statewide standard replaces today's uneven patchwork of policies.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say the measure turns eligibility into a body inspection that could subject many athletes, not just transgender ones, to invasive or expensive testing, that leaving verification to each school guarantees uneven treatment, and that excluding an at-risk group of kids from teams with their peers, down to elementary school, causes shame, isolation, and harassment.

official_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law by prohibiting surgery on a minor for the purpose of altering the minor's biological sex characteristics, and, in connection therewith, prohibiting any health-care professional or other person from knowingly performing, prescribing, administering, or providing any surgery to a minor for the purpose of altering the minor's biological sex characteristics and prohibiting the use of state or federal funds, Medicaid reimbursement, or insurance coverage to pay for this type of surgery?
plain_summary: Bans surgery on anyone under 18 when the purpose is to alter the minor's biological sex characteristics in response to the minor's perception of their sex or gender, and bans state or federal money, Medicaid, or insurance from paying for it. The ban is defined by the purpose of the surgery, not a list of procedures. Exceptions: male circumcision and treatment of medically verifiable disorders of sex development or acquired abnormalities. Non-surgical care (counseling, social transition) is not restricted.
yes_means: Surgeries on minors to alter biological sex characteristics as a response to the minor's perception of sex or gender are prohibited, and government funds and insurance cannot pay for them.
no_means: Colorado law stays as is: access to such surgeries for minors is protected, and public and private insurance may cover them.
current_law: Colorado law protects access to gender-affirming care; medically necessary gender- and sex-based surgeries may be covered by private insurance, Medicaid, or paid out of pocket. The Blue Book notes these surgeries on minors are rare (a Harvard study of 2019 claims found about 2.1 per 100,000 transgender or gender-diverse youths aged 15 to 17, 0.1 per 100,000 at ages 13 to 14, and none at 12 or under) and that Colorado's three large pediatric surgical providers (Children's Hospital Colorado, Rocky Mountain Children's, Denver Health) report they do not perform them on patients under 18.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: minimal. Small added workload for the Department of Regulatory Agencies to update rules and handle complaints, and for agencies that employ health professionals to update policies; possible legal costs. Possible small savings to Medicaid and public-employee health plans from no longer covering these surgeries. Net effect expected to be minimal.
confusing_wording_note: The title says 'modifying existing law by prohibiting surgery' and never uses 'gender-affirming' or 'transgender'; the Blue Book heading does ('in Response to Perception of Sex or Gender'). The ban hinges on purpose, so the Blue Book notes it 'may also limit other surgeries for minors, including non-transgender minors,' depending on how 'perception of sex or gender' is read. It covers surgery only, not puberty blockers, hormones, or counseling. The Blue Book also reports the major Colorado pediatric hospitals say they don't currently perform these surgeries on minors, so both sides are partly arguing about future policy rather than current practice.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say minors lack the maturity for permanent, life-altering decisions, that the most irreversible interventions should wait for adulthood like other age-restricted choices, that long-term data is lacking and some patients regret surgery, and that other states have already set similar limits.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say the ban is overly broad and could interfere with needed care for transgender and non-transgender minors alike, create uncertainty for doctors and insurers who may pull back care, and override decisions that parents, patients, and physicians all agree on, worsening mental health for transgender youth who already face stigma.

official_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes capping the state income tax rate at 4.4% of federal taxable income for individuals and corporations?
plain_summary: Writes into state law that the income tax rate for individuals and corporations may not exceed the current 4.4%, starting January 1, 2027. It does not change the current rate and does not stop future rate cuts. Its main practical effect is to conflict with Amendment 87's higher brackets if both pass.
yes_means: The current 4.4% state income tax rate becomes the maximum rate in statute.
no_means: The rate stays 4.4% with no new statutory cap.
current_law: The state income tax rate is 4.4% (set by voters in 2022). TABOR already requires voter approval for any tax rate increase. The legislature or a citizen initiative may lower the rate.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: none. The cap equals the current rate, so no change to state or local revenue or spending.
confusing_wording_note: The shortest title on the ballot and arguably the most strategic measure. By itself it changes nothing: the rate is already 4.4% and TABOR already requires a vote to raise it. Its purpose, per its own sponsor's committee name ('No on 87, Yes on 136'), is to counter Amendment 87. If both pass, the Blue Book says the measure with more yes votes is generally expected to control the conflict but the outcome is legally unclear. A statute (136) cannot normally override the constitution (87), which is part of why it's unclear. Vote consistently: Yes 136 pairs with No 87; No 136 pairs with Yes 87.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say it reinforces voters' 2022 choice to keep the rate at 4.4%, which is fair and among the lowest in the country.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it exists only to put Amendment 87 in legal jeopardy and cause a costly court fight, and that after this election it has no effect because raising rates already requires voter approval and any future approval would override it.

official_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law to increase water and land conservation funding without raising taxes, and, in connection therewith, through a voter-approved revenue change, allowing the state to keep and spend a portion of revenue from the state sales tax on sporting goods and equipment to conserve and protect Colorado's water, land, and forests, prevent wildfires, support outdoor recreation training and activities, and reduce revenue spent on these conservation purposes if necessary to preserve funding for certain tax credits?
plain_summary: Takes the state sales tax already collected on sporting goods (bikes, camping and fishing gear, boats, RVs, golf equipment, rentals, and more), about $175 million a year, and dedicates it to conservation: 47.5% to Great Outdoors Colorado (parks, trails, wildlife), 47.5% to wildfire mitigation, forest health, and watershed restoration, and 5% to outdoor recreation and access programs. It exempts that money from the TABOR cap, which reduces TABOR refunds in years when the state is over the cap. Prices and tax rates don't change.
yes_means: Existing sporting-goods sales tax revenue is directed to conservation, wildfire mitigation, and outdoor recreation programs and exempted from the state revenue limit.
no_means: That revenue stays in the general budget and subject to the TABOR limit, to be spent as the legislature decides each year or refunded to taxpayers when required.
current_law: Sales tax on sporting goods goes into the General Fund and counts toward the TABOR limit. The programs the measure would fund currently receive about $114 million: GOCO gets about $90 million a year from the lottery and no tax money; state wildfire mitigation grants about $16.4 million; watershed projects about $5 million; outdoor recreation and equity programs about $800,000.
fiscal_impact: Blue Book: moves an estimated $175.0 million in 2027-28 and $180.2 million in 2028-29 (growing with sales) from the General Fund to the named programs. In years the state is above the TABOR cap, it cuts refunds by that amount: expected to eliminate the six-tier sales tax refund in 2027-28, worth $26 to $83 per single filer and $52 to $166 per joint filer depending on income. In years below the cap, it reduces money available for other priorities (health care, education, human services). The transfer shrinks in years it would cut two income tax credits for lower-income families. If Proposition NN also passes, 137 reduces how much NN actually lets the state keep.
confusing_wording_note: 'Without raising taxes' is literally true (no rate changes) but the Blue Book's 'against' argument calls it 'a tax increase in disguise' because exempting the money from TABOR means smaller refunds in surplus years. The sporting-goods tax isn't a new or separate tax; it is the regular state sales tax on those items, redirected. 'Reduce revenue spent... to preserve funding for certain tax credits' is a safety valve protecting two low-income tax credits. Also note the interaction with Proposition NN: both let the state keep money above the TABOR cap, and 137 is paid first.

supporters_case.text: Supporters say it funds recreation access, land protection, wildfire mitigation, and watershed restoration without raising taxes or prices, through trusted programs like GOCO, at a time when the state budget is squeezed and federal support is unreliable; and that people who buy outdoor gear are natural stakeholders in protecting the outdoors.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say it is a tax increase in disguise that reduces or eliminates TABOR refunds and undermines a core taxpayer protection, that every dollar kept is a dollar less for refunds or for health care and education, and that it locks money into programs with limited accountability that already have dedicated funding, tying the legislature's hands.
